pair-01.why: A tells the scene in order (comparison, then planned revision) and lands one bold line. It has three subject options that state WIA's counter-expected decision or the reader's question, and its reply CTA names the reader. B has only two subjects and an overlong preview. It moves the revision after the principle and stacks several contrasts and abstractions ('rather than something the client's advertising had to accommodate', 'not only what we deliver', 'Respect for your existing work belongs alongside confidence'). Both tie the story straight to ELEVATE ('the standard we hold ourselves to in ELEVATE' / 'the kind of judgment we bring to ELEVATE'), which comes close to identifying the client as a member. That risk is shared, not a difference between them.

A: Caption: 'We hold every page we build to that standard before recommending it replace anything a client already has.' This widens a single scene into a universal testing protocol, which the brief says the copy does not claim.

pair-02.why: A is a real carousel: slide 1 carries the title's promise, the lines are short and stacked, the story runs over three slides and there is a 'We believe' slide. But its last slide is not a close for both readers, and its caption ends on a universal promise. B's slides are 55 to 65-word paragraphs, with no 'We believe' slide and Whitney in the third person. Its caption uses British 'recognising', piles up 'rather than' and 'without' contrasts and closes on an abstract slogan. B's only advantage is that it has a both-readers slide and makes no universal claim.

pair-03.why: The scripts are nearly identical. B's wording sounds more spoken ('Simply put,', 'a hard look', 'a fair shot', 'Both of those things can be true'), where A says 'improve our contribution'. B's caption follows problems and desires before the story: the pages couples read, the photos they scroll, the form they fill out, and the owner's real worry ('Will they respect what's already there...?'). A's caption is correct but more abstract. Both tell the planned revision as a plan.

B: Screen 2: 'We compared the page we built with the client's existing pages before replacing them.' This states or implies that the existing pages were replaced, an outcome the sources do not give, and it hints at a winning page (kept out).

pair-04.why: A's screens are specific, and a cold viewer can follow the turn from built, to compared before deciding, to planned changes with another client review. A's caption opens on a concrete reader idea, 'half of the decision', and shows what a landing page does for couples. B's second screen claims a replacement. B's caption is abstract ('the distinction between delivering an asset and deciding the role it should play') and ends on an aphoristic kicker ('The same judgment should apply to what we create and what you bring to the partnership.').

pair-05.why: The bodies are identical. A has three subject options (B has two) and a sharper preview ('The work behind a new ad shouldn't decide your answer for you.'). Its close speaks to the reader directly ('You know your brand better than anyone...'), where B's is a stiffer third-person paragraph. Both share the same weaknesses: an odd 'Their answer should be a genuine choice.' at the end of the opening paragraph, and no reply CTA.

A: Caption: after listing flaws ('The photo that doesn't capture your space. The headline that sounds a little generic...'), it says 'A client recently had that kind of reaction to some new ads from us.' Linking the client's reaction to those flaws implies the ads were poor, which the brief keeps out.

pair-06.why: A is far more readable and closer to Whitney: short stacked slides, the client's exact words in their moment, a reader's slide that names the real pull ('So you approve it and move on'), a 'We believe' slide, a both-readers close and a caption with concrete symptoms, signed. Its caption needs one clause cut to stop implying the ads were flawed, and slide 3 quotes the client, which needs the client's clearance before posting. B gets the facts right but reads like a policy memo. 'An answer can remain undecided' replaces the actual moment, the slides are paragraphs, and the caption has no story and no signature.

B: Caption: 'I welcome feedback on changes an owner would like to see, and also make clear that leaving those particular ads unused is an option.' This turns one exchange into a standing practice (a widened commitment), and 'those particular ads' has no antecedent.

pair-07.why: The scripts are identical. A's on-screen hook names the concrete subject ('Your ad team made new ads. Do you have to approve them?'). A's caption runs symptoms ('You don't want to seem difficult. You might just sign off'), then the moment told accurately, then the reframe, signed. B's hook is vaguer and its caption drops the story for an abstract stance. Both scripts already generalize ('When we send new ads for review, there are a couple of options'), and that shared widening is worth softening.

pair-08.why: B's screens are specific about what happened ('Our client wasn't sure they loved the new ads we'd made.'), so a cold viewer gets the turn. A's opening screen ('New ads we'd made were still a choice.') is ambiguous and never says what the client felt. B's caption opens on a felt problem and gives concrete details (photos, website words, inquiry replies), then the moment, then a 'We believe' reframe, signed. A's caption is abstract, has Whitney in the third person and ends on a slogan ('candor belongs in the review').

pair-09.why: The bodies are nearly identical and both keep Carmen's agreement as a recommendation. B's subject options are more concrete ('We don't exclude a competing venue from Google Ads by name alone'; 'What your team knows that your Google Ads report doesn't'). Its preview is crisp where A's is a long, stiff sentence. It adds the clarifying line 'Both were other venues, and they called for different recommendations.' Both put an Accelerator offer right after a review story, which invites the reader to infer the client is an Accelerator member. That risk is shared.

pair-10.why: Same content, but B stacks short lines and A writes 50 to 60-word paragraph slides. B has a real 'We believe' slide (A's bold line lacks it). B's caption opens with the reader's actual question ('Is that a couple who might weigh your venue too, or someone looking in a different market altogether?') and closes for both readers. A's caption is abstract ('The useful relationship brings those perspectives together rather than asking one to stand in for the other').

pair-11.why: The scripts and captions are identical except the hook and the caption's last line. A closes with a soft invitation to the reader ('If your team hears these comparisons too, we'd want that knowledge in any conversation about your ads.'). B's closing restates the point flatly. A's hook at least frames a specific client ('Their Google Ads...'), while B's reads as a generic claim. Both hooks credit Google Ads with knowledge that came from the client's team, a shared looseness. The shared script also opens in the third person rather than in Whitney's voice.

pair-12.why: The captions are effectively identical, so the screens decide it. A introduces Carmen with her role and names 'a client's search terms'. Its hook ('Some competing venue searches in Google Ads deserve a second look.') makes a clear promise to a cold viewer. B's screens drop Carmen's role ('Carmen reviewed other venue names') and use a vague 'another', and its hook is abstract ('Local knowledge mattered to a Google Ads exclusion').

B: Opening: 'I asked her to help me picture her ideal couple's wedding day, how they'd use the spaces and how the day would flow.' 'How they'd use the spaces' is added content for Whitney's prompt that the sources do not give.

pair-13.why: The bodies are identical and abstract in both ('accounts'). B wins on the first touch: three subject options, including the reader's question ('What do couples at your venue experience right now?'), and a preview that sounds human ('It just answers a different question.'). Its close speaks to the reader ('Whoever helps with your marketing should be curious...'). A has two abstract subjects, a stiff preview and a stiff close. B's opening needs the added phrase about the spaces cut to match the sources.

pair-14.why: B is stacked and readable, with a bold 'That distinction came from her.', a reader slide with concrete details (how couples arrive and move through the day), a 'We believe' slide and a warm both-readers close. Its caption opens on the reader's real situation ('you're hosting this year's weddings while picturing the next ones'). A writes paragraph slides in an abstract register ('carries different information from an account of a couple's day') with several 'rather than' and 'without' contrasts, and has no 'We believe' slide. Both say her plans kept a place in the conversation, which the later 'That's future, see?' exchange loosely supports.

pair-15.why: The scripts are identical. B's cover and hook name the concrete subject ('Your venue's vision...'; 'A venue owner asked which wedding day I wanted to hear about'), where A's hook is an ambiguous bare question for a cold viewer. B's caption opens strongly ('carrying two wedding days in your head at once'), gives concrete present-day details, tells the moment and closes for the reader. A's caption is abstract and ends flat ('we stayed with the latter rather than blending the two').

pair-16.why: B's cover speaks to the reader ('Today's wedding day, or the one you're building?') and its screens read naturally. Its caption names a felt symptom ('It's easy for those to run together... You're proud of what's happening now, and you're excited about what's coming.') before the moment. A's screens are clear, but its third screen and its caption are abstract ('remained a separate account', 'established which account we were discussing'). B's hook opens on 'Her' before the referent and its last line edges toward a slogan, but both are minor.

stance-brief-1.why: A clear first-person stance in the opening line, spoken signposts ('Here's what I mean.'), the moment as proof in a few lines, no DM kicker and a believable 60 to 75 seconds. The script is faithful: the revision stays a plan. The caption has one fidelity break that is a required fix, not optional: 'before it went back to them for review' states that the review happened, which the brief keeps out. It also has one universal-protocol line. Both are light edits.

changes.sentence: We also planned updates to our page before it went back to them for review.
changes.change: We also planned updates to our page, and I said I'd send it back to them for another look.

changes.sentence: A landing page our team builds goes into the same evaluation as the pages you already have.
changes.change: I believe a landing page our team builds should face the same questions as the pages you already have.

changes.sentence: We'd built them a landing page, and rather than moving everything over to it, we compared it with the pages they already had, because we wanted to know whether ours would convert first.
changes.change: We'd built them a landing page, and before moving everything over to it, we compared it with the pages they already had, because we wanted to know whether ours would convert first. (This keeps the piece to one contrast, after 'two separate calls'.)

stance-brief-2.why: A strong, owner-respecting stance in one breath ('I don't think the work we put into an ad should ever buy us a yes from a client.'), natural speech ('right?', 'Honestly,'), a faithful moment (not sure they loved them, review unfinished, edits welcome, no hard feelings) and no invented result. The caption follows symptoms, then belief, then story, then reframe, and is signed. The only issue is the aphorism 'yes only means something when a no was a real option', which appears in the script and again in the caption's last paragraph.

changes.sentence: Your yes only means something when a no was a real option.
changes.change: I want your yes to mean you actually want that ad in front of couples.

changes.sentence: When declining is genuinely on the table, saying yes means something.
changes.change: When you know a no is fine, the feedback gets easier to give.

stance-brief-3.why: It opens on a concrete question with a softened stance ('Honestly, I don't think a venue name can answer that on its own.'). It credits the client's team and keeps Carmen's agreement as a recommendation, with no names, places or prices. The line 'Two venue names in the same report, two different calls.' sounds spoken, and it ends gently ('We still own the advertising call.'). The caption hook adds a second 'X, not Y' on top of the script's report-versus-couple contrast, and the caption's last line leans toward a slogan.

changes.sentence: Another venue's name in your search terms is a question, not an answer.
changes.change: Seeing another venue's name in your search terms doesn't tell you whether to exclude it.

changes.sentence: Your team's knowledge of who couples compare you with is worth having in every advertising conversation.
changes.change: If your team hears which venues couples compare you with, we'd want that in the conversation about your ads.

stance-held-out-brief.why: One clear, gentle stance (vision deserves a place but shouldn't be blended into today's description). The moment is told exactly: her question, Whitney's 'current couple' answer and the fact that she raised the distinction. It claims nothing about why Whitney asked or how often WIA does this, and closes softly. Two light edits: the first line says 'she's hosting' before any owner has been introduced, and 'accounts' reads as written rather than spoken.

changes.sentence: I think a venue owner's vision for the future deserves a real place in a strategy conversation. I just don't think it should get blended into the description of the weddings she's hosting today.
changes.change: I think your vision for your venue deserves a real place in a strategy conversation. I just don't think it should get blended into the description of the weddings you're hosting today.
